sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Rotterdam is extending paid street parking to every neighbourhood inside the ring and wants a largely car-free centre. A framework from 2022 implements the coalition agreement: where parking is paid the hours run until 23:00, and paid parking is to be introduced in all neighbourhoods inside the ring, because introducing it in one district pushes parkers into the adjacent unpaid districts [3]. A recent step was sector 22 in Charlois, where paid parking began on 4 February 2026 at €2.24 an hour [6]. In the centre the street rate is €6.42 an hour, with €3.20 in the centrumring and €2.24 elsewhere [1]. In 2023 the city adopted a traffic circulation plan to make the inner city and some surrounding neighbourhoods as car-light as possible, naming Witte de Withstraat, the Meent and Nieuwe Binnenweg [8]. The new coalition plan reported in June 2026 aims for a largely car-free centre by 2040, with at least five streets fully car-free by 2030, expanded paid parking and rising parking charges [9]. That is an aim, not a decision.

In May 2024 the college decided to introduce a zero-emission zone for vans and lorries inside the ring from 1 January 2025 [10].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The municipal garages in the centre are the dearest in the city. In 2026 the city garages at Boompjes, Erasmusbrug, Kiphof, Meent, Museumpark, Oude Haven and Schouwburgplein charge €1.00 per 14 minutes by day, with a maximum of €41 per 24 hours, while other municipal garages charge €0.50 per 18 minutes with a €16 daily maximum [0]. Park-and-ride is the counterweight. RET lists 22 park-and-ride sites, most free if you continue by public transport, with Kralingse Zoom the largest at 1,700 spaces [20]. From 1 January 2025 the maximum free stay was lowered to 24 hours at Kralingse Zoom and Slinge, because about 5% of weekday use there was improper and commuters sometimes could not find a space [13]. The city plans new-build work at Kralingse Zoom and an expansion of Meijersplein between 2026 and 2030 [14]. It has also offered free public transport to weekend visitors at Meijersplein and Alexander, and reported that a similar campaign in late 2024 raised Meijersplein use by 18% [16]. Ahoy and the city have agreed to offer P+R space to event visitors, as the report notes the sites have much spare capacity outside office hours [15].

Private garages are adding supply. Q-Park opened its 18th Rotterdam garage, Rijnhaven, in 2024 with 215 public spaces at €1 per 15 minutes and a €25 daily maximum [17]. Interparking's Markthal garage has 1,040 spaces at €1.80 per 20 minutes and €35 per 24 hours [18], and Q-Park's Weena lists 480 spaces [19]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Rotterdam's garages are split between Q-Park, the city and a few others. Our price list covers 61 garages, with Q-Park running 21 (10,393 spaces), the municipality 16 (6,481) and the rest listed through ParkBee with no capacity. Prices fall with distance from the Coolsingel. Garages within 500 m have a median of €5.00 an hour, against €4.29 up to 2 km and €2.50 beyond. The municipal centre garages are priced at €4.29 an hour (the Museumpark and Schouwburgplein garages, €41 a day), and Q-Park's out-of-centre garages such as Alexandrium are €1.73.

Our measured set is four car parks with 1,737 spaces, averaging 31% on weekdays and 23% at weekends from August to early October 2026. P+R Meijersplein is the fullest (49% on weekdays, 42% at weekends), then the Q-Park Coolsingel garage (44%, 28%) and P+R Alexander (34%, 19%). P+R Beverwaard is almost unused (4%). We found no source describing these four car parks, so we say no more about them. The data cover the summer holidays, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Rotterdam.
